extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and writers interested in dramatic theory, literary criticism, and creative writing (esp. tragedy/drama)
extracted.subtask_description: Applying Aristotle's Poetics as a practical set of criteria for composing or evaluating tragic drama: focuses on plot, character, catharsis, diction, melody, spectacle, and related devices (recognition, reversal, hamartia, unity). Useful for playwrights, critics, and students of narrative craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Tragedy is a representation of a serious, complete action that has magnitude, in embellished speech, with each of its elements [used] separately in the [various] parts [of the play] and [represented] by people acting and not by narration, accomplished using pity and terror the catharsis of such emotions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Embellished speech’ means rhythm and melody (song); elements may be expressed separately (some parts by spoken verse, others by song). The representation should be enacted, not merely narrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (mythos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot refers to the “organization of incidents”. It should imitate an action that evokes pity and fear and involve a change (from bad to good or good to bad). Complex plots have reversals (peripeteia) and recognitions (anagnorisis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best plots include reversals and recognitions and may involve suffering/violence, especially between friends and family. The most tragic plot often pushes a good character toward undeserved misfortune because of a mistake (hamartia). Actions in the plot should follow logically from preceding events and from character; recognitions and reversals are most satisfying when they are seen afterwards as plausible or necessary consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (ethos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral character of agents reveals a tragedy’s success: in a perfect tragedy, character supports the plot so that motivations and traits connect parts of the cause-and-effect chain producing pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main characters should be: Good (not at moral extremes), Appropriate (fitting age/status/role), Consistent (actions follow the law of probability and necessity). If a character changes, causes should be shown; ‘consistently inconsistent’ behaviour must be made intelligible to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dianoia is the spoken reasoning of human characters that can explain characters or story background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poet/playwright should express thought through characters' words and actions so that ideas are embodied in dramatic behaviour rather than abstract exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (lexis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lexis refers to the quality of speech in tragedy; speeches should reflect character and express the meaning of the words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translation issues noted (lexis better rendered as ‘speech’ or ‘language’). Diction must be appropriate to the character and occasion, and helps reveal thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody (melos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Melos (often ‘melody’ or ‘music-dance’) is the musical element of dramatic composition and is part of the material of poetry alongside language and rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Melos can encompass music and dance (the chorus’ performance). Musical and movement elements should be integrated with plot and speech to contribute to the drama’s effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as actor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be written as one of the actors: an integral part of the whole that takes a share in the action and contributes to the unity of the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the Chorus as participant rather than mere ornament; it should contribute to the pleasure of the drama and help unify the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (opsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle refers to the visual apparatus of the play (set, costumes, props) and is called the 'least artistic' element of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle is ‘the least connected with the work of the poet’; beautiful visuals cannot compensate for bad acting or a bad story. Spectacle should support, not substitute for, plot and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis (tragic pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic pleasure, or catharsis, experienced by fear and pity should be produced in the spectator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The aim is effecting the proper catharsis of these emotions—design plot, character, and performance to elicit fear and pity and thereby produce the cathartic response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia and Anagnorisis (reversal and recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversals (peripeteia) and recognitions (anagnorisis) are key plot devices that evoke tragic emotions and appear in complex plots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most satisfying reversals and recognitions are those that occur as plausible consequences of prior actions; late discoveries (almost done in ignorance but discovered at the last moment) are judged especially effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia (mistake/tragic error)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamartia is a mistake or miscalculation: the most tragic plots often involve a good character being pushed toward undeserved misfortune because of such an error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plots centered on hamartia are more tragic than those with simple moral oppositions; the mistake should be credible in light of character and circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and magnitude of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should represent a serious, complete action of a certain magnitude; poetic narratives are unified by a plot whose logic binds constituent elements by necessity and probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity (single, concentrated action) is a virtue of tragedy: a more concentrated effect (less time, greater unity) is more pleasurable than a dispersed epic imitation. Epic may have plurality of actions; tragedy’s unity is artistically superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matter of poetry: language, rhythm, and melody
rubrics_metrics.description: Language, rhythm, and melody make up the matter of poetic creation: the epic uses language alone; lyric and drama may blend language with rhythm and melody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize which materials your form requires (e.g., drama typically involves music/dance, chorus, and speech) and compose accordingly. Translation/interpretation issues (e.g., 'rhuthmos') affect how these terms map to modern craft concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects/agents and social status (tripartite division)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle distinguishes character types relative to the audience: superior to the audience, inferior, or at the same level; tragedy deals with serious, important, and virtuous people while comedy treats less virtuous foibles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose characters whose social/ethical standing is appropriate to the genre: tragic subjects are typically of higher station or virtue to produce pity/fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of imitation (narration vs direct speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: One may imitate agents via a narrator throughout, partly (direct speech in parts and a narrator in parts), or only by direct speech using actors; tragedy uses actors speaking lines directly (no narrator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the story is best shown or told; tragedy’s power lies in enacted speech and action rather than narrated summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot construction practice: visualization, complication, dénouement
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should visualize all scenes when creating the plot and incorporate complication and dénouement within the story, combining all elements of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan scenes holistically; include complications that lead toward a coherent dénouement. Ensure discovery and reversals are placed to maximize emotional and logical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical necessity and probability in action
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions should follow logically from the situation created by prior events and from the character of the agent; the Law of Probability and Necessity governs plausibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even surprising events should, in retrospect, feel like necessary or probable outcomes; maintain internal causal logic so surprises feel satisfying rather than arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressing theme through action and diction
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must express thought (themes, ideas) through the characters' words and actions while paying close attention to diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid telling themes directly; instead let characters’ choices, speeches, and interactions embody the thematic material, with diction tuned to reveal meaning and moral qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative importance of elements (spectacle least, plot most)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle ranks the elements of tragedy, treating spectacle as the least artistic/least connected with the poet and plot/mythos as primary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize plot, character, and diction over visual show; use spectacle only to support the central dramatic elements rather than compensate for weakness in them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison: tragedy vs epic
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is artistically superior to epic: tragedy has everything the epic has (and the epic meter is admissible) but achieves a more concentrated effect and unity in less time; the epic’s plurality of actions dilutes unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing form, remember the trade-offs: epic allows breadth and multiplicity of actions; tragedy seeks concentrated ethical and emotional effect through unity and immediacy.
